newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy government approves year-end fiscal package.
newsitem.headline: Italy government approves year-end fiscal package.

text.p: The Italian government on Monday approved an end-of-year package of measures intended to raise around 4.3 trillion lire ($2.8 billion) and complete the country's 1997 austerity budget.

"The fiscal measures, as laid out in the budget law, complete therefore the 1997 budget through the raising of extra income for a total of 4.305 trillion lire," the government said in a statement after a cabinet meeting.
It said the measures, adopted in the overall form of a decree law, followed two main criteria -- to avoid contributing to inflation and avoid hitting consumer demand.

The statement said the measures also aimed to provide limited help for struggling industrial sectors to the tune of a total 1.78 trillion lire ($1.17 billion) and to bring Italy more in line with European tax regulations.
It said the main revenue-raising actions focused on advance excise duties -- mainly on mineral oils, alcoholic beverages, methane gas and electricity -- and measures against tax evasion.
Forcing companies to speed up payments of certain excise duties is expected to raise around two trillion lire ($1.3 billion) in 1997.
Prime Minister Romano Prodi told a news conference that the package would have no inflationary effect and would stimulate production and reduce tax pressure on parts of industry.
The measures included incentives to scrap cars more than 10 years old in an effort to boost the flagging car sector.
Value added tax on beef, pork and salami products was reduced temporarily from 16 to 10 percent while the tax on certain types of medicines was raised from four to 10 percent.

Duty on petrol, unleaded and leaded, remained unchanged but a rise of 22 lire on the price of a litre of unleaded petrol, introduced provisionally in 1996 to help pay for the costs of Italy's mission in Bosnia, would remain in force for 1997.
The 1997 budget was approved last weekend, giving Prodi's government a free hand to work out the details of how the final 4.3 trillion lire would be brought in.

The government is fighting to reduce the ratio between the public sector deficit and gross domestic product (GDP) to the three percent level demanded by the Maastricht treaty for countries wishing to join the planned European single currency.

Many economists believe that the government will have to prepare a mini-budget in early 1997 if the three percent threshold is to be reached next year. The ratio is expected to be just over seven percent this year.
